content: Sodium chloride, commonly referred to as table salt, salt, or halite, is a chemical compound with the molecular formula NaCl. It is the primary contributor to the salinity of the ocean and the extracellular fluid in many multicellular organisms. As the main component of edible salt, it is widely used as a seasoning and food preservative. Salt is primarily produced through the evaporation of seawater or brine from sources such as brine wells and salt lakes, as well as by mining rock salt, also known as halite. While its culinary uses are well-known, salt is also utilized in a variety of industrial applications, including the production of pulp and paper, setting dyes in textiles, and manufacturing soaps and detergents. In colder regions, such as most of Canada and the northern United States, large quantities of rock salt are used to de-ice roads during winter. However, road salt becomes ineffective at temperatures below -15°C to -20°C (5°F to -4°F). Salt serves as a raw material for the production of chlorine, which is essential for manufacturing modern materials such as PVC and pesticides. Industrially, elemental chlorine is typically produced via the electrolysis of sodium chloride dissolved in water. This process, known as the chlor-alkali process, also generates hydrogen gas and sodium hydroxide. Sodium metal is commercially produced through the electrolysis of molten sodium chloride in a Downs cell, where calcium chloride is added to lower the melting point below 700°C. Since calcium is more electropositive than sodium, no calcium is deposited at the cathode. This method is more cost-effective than the older process of electrolyzing sodium hydroxide. Sodium chloride is also used in other chemical processes for the large-scale production of compounds containing sodium or chlorine. For example, in the Solvay process, sodium chloride is used to produce sodium carbonate and calcium chloride. In the Mannheim and Hargreaves processes, it is employed to produce sodium sulfate and hydrochloric acid. Biologically, many microorganisms cannot survive in highly saline environments because water is drawn out of their cells through osmosis. This property makes salt an effective preservative for certain foods, such as smoked bacon or fish. Salt can also be used to remove leeches that have attached themselves to a host. Historically, it has been employed to disinfect wounds. During medieval times, salt was even rubbed into household surfaces as a cleaning agent.
